decks.title: Matrices — Part 1: Matrices, types and operations
goals: Write data as a matrix and state its order
Construct a matrix from a rule for its general element
Identify row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, identity and zero matrices
Use equality of matrices to find unknowns
Add, subtract, scalar-multiply and multiply matrices, and show that AB need not equal BA

slides.heading: Matrices, Part 1: Arranging numbers in rows and columns
slides.body_md: A matrix is a rectangle of numbers that we can add, scale and multiply.

visual.alt: Table of a sports shop stock: branch P has 25 bats, 40 balls and 15 helmets; branch Q has 30 bats, 20 balls and 35 helmets.
visual.caption: The same data as the $2 \times 3$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 25 & 40 & 15 \\ 30 & 20 & 35 \end{bmatrix}$.

slides.narration: Welcome to matrices. Shopkeepers, coaches and engineers all keep numbers in rows and columns. On the screen, a sports shop records the stock of two branches: one row for each branch, one column for each item. Write that table inside square brackets and you have a matrix. In this part you will learn the language of matrices and how to calculate with them.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Write data as a **matrix** and give its **order**
Build a matrix from a rule such as $a_{ij} = 3i - j$
Add, scale and **multiply** matrices; see why $AB \ne BA$
slides.narration: Here are your goals for part one. By the end you will be able to read and build matrices, name their types, find unknowns from equal matrices, and carry out every operation, including multiplication, which follows a rule of its own. Multiplication is where most marks are won and lost, so we will practise it carefully.

slides.heading: What is a matrix?
slides.body_md: A **matrix** is a rectangular arrangement of numbers (its **elements** or **entries**) in rows and columns, enclosed in brackets. We name matrices with capital letters.

visual.alt: Table of a sports shop stock: branch P has 25 bats, 40 balls and 15 helmets; branch Q has 30 bats, 20 balls and 35 helmets.
visual.caption: The same data as the $2 \times 3$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 25 & 40 & 15 \\ 30 & 20 & 35 \end{bmatrix}$.

slides.narration: A matrix is simply numbers arranged in rows and columns inside brackets. Rows run across, columns run down. This matrix S holds the shop data. Its first row is branch P, its second row is branch Q, and its three columns are bats, balls and helmets. Every number has a fixed place, and that place carries meaning.

slides.heading: Order and the general element
slides.body_md: A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns has **order** $m \times n$ and $mn$ elements. The element in row $i$ and column $j$ is written $a_{ij}$, and the matrix as $A = [a_{ij}]_{m \times n}$.

visual.alt: Grid showing the position of each element of a 2 by 3 matrix: row 1 holds a 1 1, a 1 2, a 1 3 and row 2 holds a 2 1, a 2 2, a 2 3. The first index is the row, the second the column.
visual.caption: $a_{ij}$: row $i$ first, column $j$ second.

slides.narration: The order of a matrix is rows by columns, always in that order. The shop matrix is two by three and has six elements. To point at one element we use two subscripts: the first is the row, the second is the column. So a two three sits in row two, column three. Mixing up the two subscripts is the most common slip in this chapter.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: build a matrix from a rule
slides.body_md: Construct the $2 \times 3$ matrix $A = [a_{ij}]$ with $a_{ij} = 3i - j$.

visual.alt: Table computing a i j equals 3 i minus j: row 1 gives 2, 1, 0 and row 2 gives 5, 4, 3.
visual.caption: Fill the grid one cell at a time: $a_{ij} = 3i - j$.

slides.narration: When a matrix is defined by a rule, fill it one cell at a time. Hold the row number fixed and run through the columns. In row one, i is one, so each entry is three minus the column number: two, one, zero. In row two, i is two, so the entries are six minus the column number: five, four, three. Write the answer neatly in brackets.

slides.heading: Types of matrices
slides.body_md: Matrices are named by their shape and by where their non-zero entries sit.

visual.alt: Table of the types of matrices with a condition and an example for each: row matrix with one row, column matrix with one column, square matrix with as many rows as columns, diagonal matrix with zeros off the diagonal, scalar matrix with equal diagonal entries, identity matrix with ones on the diagonal, and zero matrix with every entry zero.
visual.caption: Every identity matrix is scalar, and every scalar matrix is diagonal.

slides.narration: Here are the types you must know. A row matrix has one row, a column matrix one column. A square matrix has as many rows as columns. A square matrix with zeros everywhere off the main diagonal is diagonal. If the diagonal entries are also equal, it is a scalar matrix, and if they all equal one, it is the identity matrix, written I. A zero matrix has every entry zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the matrix
slides.body_md: Choose the best name for the matrix.
slides.narration: Look at the shape first, then at the entries off the diagonal, then at the diagonal entries themselves. Pick the most precise name that fits.

slides.heading: Naming a square matrix step by step
slides.body_md: Each special square matrix is a special case of the one before it.

visual.alt: Decision chart for naming a matrix: if it is not square it is a row, column or rectangular matrix; if square, check whether all off-diagonal entries are zero; if not, it is just square; if yes, check whether the diagonal entries are equal: if not, it is diagonal; if yes, it is a scalar matrix, and the identity when the common value is 1.
visual.caption: Square → diagonal → scalar → identity: each is a special case of the one before.

slides.narration: This chart turns naming into three questions. Is it square? Are all the entries off the diagonal zero? Are the diagonal entries equal? Answer them in order. Notice the nesting: every identity matrix is a scalar matrix, and every scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix. So the identity matrix earns all three names, but the most precise name is the one examiners want.

slides.heading: Equality of matrices
slides.body_md: Two matrices are **equal** when they have the **same order** and every pair of corresponding entries is equal.

nodes.label: Equate each pair of corresponding entries

visual.alt: Flow for equality of matrices: if the orders differ, the matrices are not equal; if the orders match, equate corresponding entries and solve the equations that result.
visual.caption: Two matrices are equal only when they have the same order and the same entries.

slides.narration: Two matrices are equal only if they have the same order and the same entry in every position. So one matrix equation gives you one ordinary equation for each position. This is how board questions hide unknowns inside matrices: equate entries, then solve the small equations that appear.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: unknowns from equality
slides.body_md: Find $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ if $\begin{bmatrix} 2a & b + 1 \\ c - 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ 7 & d \end{bmatrix}$.

nodes.label: Equate each pair of corresponding entries

visual.alt: Flow for equality of matrices: if the orders differ, the matrices are not equal; if the orders match, equate corresponding entries and solve the equations that result.
visual.caption: Two matrices are equal only when they have the same order and the same entries.

slides.narration: Both matrices are two by two, so they can be equal. Match each position. Two a equals six gives a equals three. b plus one equals minus three gives b equals minus four. c minus two equals seven gives c equals nine. And the bottom right gives d equals four. Four positions, four small equations.

slides.heading: Adding matrices and multiplying by a scalar
slides.body_md: For matrices of the **same order**: $A + B$ adds corresponding entries; $kA$ multiplies every entry by $k$; $A - B = A + (-1)B$.

visual.alt: Table of one canteen sales: Monday 60 samosas, 45 idlis and 30 juices; Tuesday 55, 50 and 35; the total row 115, 95 and 65 is obtained by adding corresponding entries.
visual.caption: Adding matrices adds corresponding entries.

slides.narration: Addition is natural. A canteen records Monday and Tuesday sales in matrices of the same shape. Adding corresponding entries gives the two day totals. Multiplying a matrix by a number, called a scalar, multiplies every entry. Subtraction is adding the negative. Matrices of different orders cannot be added at all.

slides.heading: Properties of addition and scalar multiplication
slides.body_md: Because these operations act entry by entry, they obey the familiar laws of numbers.

rows: $k(A + B) = kA + kB$, $(k + l)A = kA + lA$

visual.alt: Table of properties of addition and scalar multiplication for matrices of the same order: commutative, associative, the zero matrix as identity, negative matrix as inverse, and scalars distributing over sums.
visual.caption: Addition behaves just like addition of numbers, entry by entry.

slides.narration: Since addition works entry by entry, it inherits the laws of ordinary numbers. It is commutative and associative. The zero matrix changes nothing when added, and every matrix has a negative that cancels it. Scalars distribute over sums of matrices and over sums of scalars. You may use these laws freely, as long as the orders match.

slides.heading: Multiplication: when is AB defined?
slides.body_md: If $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times p$, then $AB$ is defined and is $m \times p$. If the inner numbers differ, $AB$ is **not defined**.

visual.alt: Flow for when a product is defined: A of order m by n and B of order n by p have matching inner numbers, so A B exists and has order m by p, the outer numbers.
visual.caption: Inner numbers must match; outer numbers give the order.

slides.narration: Multiplication needs a check before any arithmetic. Write the two orders side by side. The inner numbers, the columns of the first matrix and the rows of the second, must match. If they do, the outer numbers give the order of the product. A two by three matrix times a three by two matrix gives a two by two matrix.

slides.heading: Row times column
slides.body_md: Entry $(i, j)$ of $AB$ is found by multiplying the entries of **row $i$ of $A$** with the matching entries of **column $j$ of $B$** and adding.

visual.alt: Table showing how the entry in row 1, column 2 of A B is found: row 1 of A, which is 1, minus 2, 3, is paired with column 2 of B, which is 1, 0, 3; multiplying pairs and adding gives 1 plus 0 plus 9, which is 10.
visual.caption: Entry $(i, j)$ of $AB$ = row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$.

slides.narration: Each entry of a product comes from one row of the first matrix and one column of the second. Pair them up, first with first, second with second, and so on. Multiply each pair and add the results. For row one and column two in our example, one times one, plus minus two times zero, plus three times three, gives ten.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a product of non-square matrices
slides.body_md: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Find $AB$.

visual.alt: Table showing how the entry in row 1, column 2 of A B is found: row 1 of A, which is 1, minus 2, 3, is paired with column 2 of B, which is 1, 0, 3; multiplying pairs and adding gives 1 plus 0 plus 9, which is 10.
visual.caption: Entry $(i, j)$ of $AB$ = row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$.

slides.narration: Check the orders first: two by three times three by two is defined, and the answer is two by two. Now four row by column sums. Row one with column one gives minus three. Row one with column two gives ten. Row two gives three and three. Interestingly, B times A is also defined, but it is three by three, so it cannot possibly equal A times B.

slides.heading: Quick check: order of a product
slides.body_md: Decide whether the product exists, and its order.
slides.narration: Write the two orders next to each other. Compare the inner numbers, and if they match, read the outer numbers.

slides.heading: Order matters: AB and BA
slides.body_md: Even for square matrices, $AB$ and $BA$ are usually **different**. Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**.

visual.alt: Table of the products A B and B A for A with rows 1 1 and 0 2 and B with rows 3 0 and 1 1: A B has rows 4 1 and 2 2, while B A has rows 3 3 and 1 3, so the two products are different.
visual.caption: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: order matters.

slides.narration: Take two simple two by two matrices and multiply them both ways. A times B and B times A come out different. This is the single biggest change from ordinary numbers. Always keep the order in which matrices are written, and never swap them to make a calculation easier. When two particular matrices do give the same product both ways, we say they commute.

slides.heading: A matrix moves points
slides.body_md: A $2 \times 2$ matrix times a column $\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}$ gives a new column: a new point. $M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ sends $(1, 1)$ to $(3, 1)$.

visual.alt: The unit square with corners O at the origin, P at 1 comma 0, Q at 1 comma 1 and R at 0 comma 1, shaded, and its image under the matrix with rows 2 1 and 0 1: a slanted parallelogram with corners O, P prime at 2 comma 0, Q prime at 3 comma 1 and R prime at 1 comma 1, which is the same point as Q.
visual.caption: Multiplying each corner by $M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ stretches and slants the square into a parallelogram.

slides.narration: Here is a picture of multiplication. Treat each corner of the unit square as a column with two entries and multiply it by the matrix M. The corner one comma one goes to three comma one, and one comma zero goes to two comma zero. The square becomes a slanted parallelogram. Computer graphics move shapes on a screen in exactly this way.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a matrix polynomial
slides.body_md: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, show that $A^2 - 5A + 7I = O$.

visual.alt: Table building A squared minus 5 A plus 7 I for A with rows 3 1 and minus 1 2: A squared has rows 8 5 and minus 5 3; minus 5 A has rows minus 15 minus 5 and 5 minus 10; 7 I has 7 on the diagonal; adding gives the zero matrix.
visual.caption: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2 - 5A + 7I = O$.

slides.narration: A matrix polynomial replaces x by the matrix and the constant term by a multiple of the identity matrix. First square A by multiplying it by itself, not by squaring each entry. Then work out five A and seven I. Combine position by position, and every entry is zero. We will reuse this relation in part two to find the inverse of A.

slides.heading: Properties of multiplication
slides.body_md: Some laws of numbers survive; others fail.

visual.alt: Table of properties of matrix multiplication: associative yes, distributive yes, identity yes for square matrices; commutative not in general; the zero-product rule fails; and the square of a sum expands with 2 A B only when A and B commute.
visual.caption: Three rules carry over from numbers; three do not.

slides.narration: Matrix multiplication is associative and distributes over addition, and the identity matrix behaves like the number one. But three habits from ordinary algebra fail. A times B need not equal B times A. A product can be the zero matrix even when neither factor is zero. And the square of a sum has a middle term of A B plus B A, not two A B.

slides.heading: Quick check: square a matrix
slides.body_md: Square the given matrix correctly.
slides.narration: Squaring means multiplying the matrix by itself, row by column. It does not mean squaring each entry. Work out each of the four entries before choosing.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Order $m \times n$: rows first; $a_{ij}$ is in row $i$, column $j$
Types: row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, identity, zero
Equal matrices: same order and equal corresponding entries
Add and scale entry by entry (same order only)
$AB$ needs inner orders to match; $AB \ne BA$ in general

nodes.label: Types: row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, identity, zero
Add, subtract, scale: same order, entry by entry
Multiply: row times column; $AB \ne BA$ in general

visual.alt: Summary chain for part one: a matrix has an order and entries; matrices come in several types; addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication work entry by entry on matrices of the same order; multiplication pairs rows with columns and is not commutative.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: To sum up. A matrix has an order, rows by columns, and each element has a row and column address. Square matrices come in special types. Equal matrices let you set up equations. Addition and scalar multiplication work entry by entry. Multiplication pairs rows with columns, needs matching inner orders, and depends on the order of the factors.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Construct a matrix (2 marks):** correct entries row by row
**Products (2–5 marks):** order check, each row-by-column sum shown, final matrix
**Matrix polynomial (2–3 marks):** $A^2$ correct 1 + other terms 1 + simplified result 1
**Mistake:** squaring each entry instead of computing $AA$
**Mistake:** writing $7$ instead of $7I$ for the constant term

visual.alt: Table of properties of matrix multiplication: associative yes, distributive yes, identity yes for square matrices; commutative not in general; the zero-product rule fails; and the square of a sum expands with 2 A B only when A and B commute.
visual.caption: Three rules carry over from numbers; three do not.

slides.narration: Show the order check before multiplying; it earns credit and avoids impossible products. Write out each row by column sum, because a single arithmetic slip then costs only one mark. In matrix polynomials, the constant must become a multiple of the identity matrix. And never square entries one by one when a question asks for A squared.

decks.title: Matrices — Part 2: Transpose, symmetric matrices and inverses
goals: Find the transpose of a matrix and use its four properties
Express a square matrix as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix
Define an invertible matrix and prove that its inverse is unique
Find or verify the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix using AB = BA = I

slides.heading: Matrices, Part 2: Transpose and inverse
slides.body_md: Flip a matrix in its diagonal, and undo a matrix with its inverse.

visual.alt: A 2 by 3 matrix with rows 1 4 0 and minus 2 3 5, and its transpose, a 3 by 2 matrix whose columns are those rows: rows 1 minus 2, 4 3 and 0 5.
visual.caption: Rows of $A$ become columns of $A^T$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. We meet two new operations. The first, the transpose, turns rows into columns, and it leads to symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices. The second, the inverse, undoes what a matrix does, just as dividing undoes multiplying. Both appear in almost every board paper, often as proofs.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **transpose** $A^T$ and use its properties
Split any square matrix into these two parts
Find or verify the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. Notice that two of them are proofs. Proofs in this chapter are short, usually three or four lines, and they rely on the properties of the transpose and on the definition of the inverse. Learn those properties exactly.

slides.heading: The transpose
slides.body_md: The **transpose** $A^T$ (also written $A'$) of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is the $n \times m$ matrix whose rows are the columns of $A$: if $A = [a_{ij}]$ then $A^T = [a_{ji}]$.

visual.alt: A 2 by 3 matrix with rows 1 4 0 and minus 2 3 5, and its transpose, a 3 by 2 matrix whose columns are those rows: rows 1 minus 2, 4 3 and 0 5.
visual.caption: Rows of $A$ become columns of $A^T$.

slides.narration: To transpose a matrix, write its first row as the first column, its second row as the second column, and so on. A two by three matrix becomes three by two. The entry in row i, column j moves to row j, column i. Picture the matrix flipping over its main diagonal.

slides.heading: Properties of the transpose
slides.body_md: For matrices of suitable orders and any scalar $k$:

visual.alt: Table of the four properties of the transpose: transposing twice returns A; a scalar comes out; the transpose of a sum is the sum of transposes; the transpose of a product is the product of transposes in the reverse order.
visual.caption: The order reverses only for products.

slides.narration: Four properties do almost all the work. Transposing twice brings you back. Scalars come outside. The transpose of a sum is the sum of the transposes. And the transpose of a product is the product of the transposes in reverse order. That reversal is not optional. With the original order the product may not even be defined.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the reversal law
slides.body_md: Verify $(AB)^T = B^TA^T$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$.

visual.alt: Table of the four properties of the transpose: transposing twice returns A; a scalar comes out; the transpose of a sum is the sum of transposes; the transpose of a product is the product of transposes in the reverse order.
visual.caption: The order reverses only for products.

slides.narration: Work out each side on its own. On the left, multiply A by B first, then transpose. On the right, transpose each matrix first, then multiply them in the reverse order. Both give the matrix with rows four six and seven minus three. Keep the two sides separate in your working, so the examiner can see the verification.

slides.heading: Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
slides.body_md: A square matrix is **symmetric** if $A^T = A$ and **skew-symmetric** if $A^T = -A$. In a skew-symmetric matrix every diagonal entry is $0$, because $a_{ii} = -a_{ii}$.

visual.alt: Table comparing symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices: symmetric means the transpose equals the matrix, mirror entries equal, example with rows 2 minus 1 4, minus 1 0 3, 4 3 5; skew-symmetric means the transpose equals the negative, mirror entries opposite and diagonal zero, example with rows 0 2 minus 6, minus 2 0 1, 6 minus 1 0.
visual.caption: Mirror the matrix in its main diagonal: equal partners or opposite partners.

slides.narration: Fold a square matrix along its main diagonal. If each entry lands on an equal partner, the matrix is symmetric. If each entry lands on its negative, the matrix is skew-symmetric. In that case each diagonal entry is its own partner, so it equals its own negative, and must be zero. That gives a quick first test.

slides.heading: Quick check: skew-symmetric diagonal
slides.body_md: What must the diagonal of a skew-symmetric matrix be?
slides.narration: Use the condition a j i equals minus a i j, and put j equal to i.

slides.heading: Splitting a square matrix
slides.body_md: For any square $A$: $A + A^T$ is symmetric and $A - A^T$ is skew-symmetric. Halving each and adding returns $A$.

visual.alt: Flow for splitting a square matrix: find A transpose; half of A plus A transpose is the symmetric part P; half of A minus A transpose is the skew-symmetric part Q; and P plus Q gives back A.
visual.caption: Every square matrix splits into a symmetric part and a skew-symmetric part.

slides.narration: Here is a powerful fact. Add a square matrix to its transpose and the result is always symmetric. Subtract the transpose and the result is always skew-symmetric. Take half of each. Their sum is exactly A, because the transposes cancel. So every square matrix is a symmetric part plus a skew-symmetric part.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: split a matrix
slides.body_md: Express $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ as $P + Q$ with $P$ symmetric and $Q$ skew-symmetric.

visual.alt: Flow for splitting a square matrix: find A transpose; half of A plus A transpose is the symmetric part P; half of A minus A transpose is the skew-symmetric part Q; and P plus Q gives back A.
visual.caption: Every square matrix splits into a symmetric part and a skew-symmetric part.

slides.narration: First write the transpose. Then add and halve to get P, and subtract and halve to get Q. P has equal mirror entries, four and four, so it is symmetric. Q has zeros on the diagonal and opposite mirror entries, so it is skew-symmetric. Always finish by adding P and Q to check that you get A back.

slides.heading: Why the split always works
slides.body_md: The proof uses only the transpose properties.

visual.alt: Table of the four properties of the transpose: transposing twice returns A; a scalar comes out; the transpose of a sum is the sum of transposes; the transpose of a product is the product of transposes in the reverse order.
visual.caption: The order reverses only for products.

slides.narration: The proof takes three lines. Transpose A plus A transpose: you get A transpose plus A, the same matrix, so it is symmetric. Transpose A minus A transpose: you get its negative, so it is skew-symmetric. Halving does not spoil either property. And the halves add up to A. Board papers often ask for exactly this proof.

slides.heading: Quick check: the symmetric part
slides.body_md: Find the symmetric part of the given matrix.
slides.narration: Add the matrix to its transpose, then halve every entry. Watch out for options that forget the half.

slides.heading: Invertible matrices
slides.body_md: A square matrix $A$ of order $n$ is **invertible** if there is a square matrix $B$ of order $n$ with $AB = BA = I$. Then $B$ is the **inverse** of $A$, written $A^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of two square matrices: for the matrix with rows 4 3 and 1 1, the candidate with rows 1 minus 3 and minus 1 4 gives the identity both ways, so it is the inverse; the matrix with rows 1 2 and 2 4 sends the non-zero column 2, minus 1 to zero, so it has no inverse.
visual.caption: A matrix that sends a non-zero column to $O$ cannot be undone, so it has no inverse.

slides.narration: For numbers, five times one fifth is one. For matrices the role of one is played by the identity matrix. If some matrix B gives the identity when multiplied by A on either side, B is the inverse of A. Only square matrices can have inverses, and not all of them do. The matrix in the second row sends a non-zero column to zero, so nothing can undo it.

slides.heading: The inverse is unique
slides.body_md: If $B$ and $C$ are both inverses of $A$, then $B = C$.

nodes.label: Suppose $B$ and $C$ are both inverses of $A$
So $B = C$: the inverse is unique

visual.alt: Proof chain for uniqueness of the inverse: start with B equals B times I, replace I by A C, regroup as B A times C by associativity, which is I times C, which is C; so B equals C.
visual.caption: Four short steps prove the inverse is unique.

slides.narration: Can a matrix have two different inverses? No. Suppose B and C are both inverses. Start with B equals B times I. Replace I by A times C. Regroup, using associativity, as B times A, times C. But B times A is I, so this is I times C, which is C. So B and C are the same matrix. Learn these four steps; they make a three mark proof.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: verify an inverse
slides.body_md: Show that $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ is the inverse of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

visual.alt: Table of two square matrices: for the matrix with rows 4 3 and 1 1, the candidate with rows 1 minus 3 and minus 1 4 gives the identity both ways, so it is the inverse; the matrix with rows 1 2 and 2 4 sends the non-zero column 2, minus 1 to zero, so it has no inverse.
visual.caption: A matrix that sends a non-zero column to $O$ cannot be undone, so it has no inverse.

slides.narration: To verify an inverse, multiply. A times B gives the identity matrix. Then B times A also gives the identity matrix. Strictly, the definition asks for both products, so show both. Once they are both I, you may write B equals A inverse with confidence.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: find an inverse from AB = I
slides.body_md: Find the inverse of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ by writing $B = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix}$ and solving $AB = I$.

visual.alt: Table solving A B equals I for A with rows 2 5 and 1 3: the first column gives 2 p plus 5 r equals 1 and p plus 3 r equals 0, so r is minus 1 and p is 3; the second column gives 2 q plus 5 s equals 0 and q plus 3 s equals 1, so s is 2 and q is minus 5.
visual.caption: So the inverse is $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

slides.narration: Without any special formula, we can find an inverse by solving equations. Let the unknown inverse have entries p, q, r and s. Multiplying A by it and setting the result equal to I gives two small pairs of linear equations, one for each column. Solve them, then check by multiplying in the other order.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: inverse from a matrix relation
slides.body_md: From part 1, $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2 - 5A + 7I = O$. Find $A^{-1}$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** So $A \cdot \frac17(5I - A) = I$, and likewise $\frac17(5I - A) \cdot A = I$.

visual.alt: Table building A squared minus 5 A plus 7 I for A with rows 3 1 and minus 1 2: A squared has rows 8 5 and minus 5 3; minus 5 A has rows minus 15 minus 5 and 5 minus 10; 7 I has 7 on the diagonal; adding gives the zero matrix.
visual.caption: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2 - 5A + 7I = O$.

notes.title: Matrices — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Matrices, order and the general element
sections.body_md:
A **matrix** is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns. A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns has **order** $m \times n$ and $mn$ elements. The element in row $i$, column $j$ is $a_{ij}$; we write $A = [a_{ij}]_{m \times n}$.

Matrices organise information. The stock of two shop branches across three items is a $2 \times 3$ matrix, and each entry's position tells you its meaning.

**From a rule:** to construct $A$ with $a_{ij} = 3i - j$ ($2 \times 3$), fix the row and run through the columns: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A rectangular array of numbers in rows and columns.
$m \times n$: number of rows, then number of columns.
The entry in row $i$ and column $j$.

visual.alt: Grid showing the position of each element of a 2 by 3 matrix: row 1 holds a 1 1, a 1 2, a 1 3 and row 2 holds a 2 1, a 2 2, a 2 3. The first index is the row, the second the column.
visual.caption: $a_{ij}$: row $i$ first, column $j$ second.

visuals.alt: Table of a sports shop stock: branch P has 25 bats, 40 balls and 15 helmets; branch Q has 30 bats, 20 balls and 35 helmets.
visuals.caption: The same data as the $2 \times 3$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 25 & 40 & 15 \\ 30 & 20 & 35 \end{bmatrix}$.

sections.heading: 2. Types of matrices
sections.body_md:
- **Row matrix:** one row ($1 \times n$). **Column matrix:** one column ($m \times 1$).
- **Square matrix:** $m = n$. Its **main diagonal** is $a_{11}, a_{22}, \dots, a_{nn}$.
- **Diagonal matrix:** square, with $a_{ij} = 0$ whenever $i \ne j$.
- **Scalar matrix:** diagonal with all diagonal entries equal to some $k$; it equals $kI$.
- **Identity matrix** $I_n$: diagonal entries $1$, others $0$.
- **Zero matrix** $O$: every entry $0$ (any order).

Every identity matrix is scalar, and every scalar matrix is diagonal.

key_terms.definition_md: A square matrix whose off-diagonal entries are all zero.
A diagonal matrix with equal diagonal entries, $kI$.
The scalar matrix with $1$ on the diagonal, written $I$.

visual.alt: Table of the types of matrices with a condition and an example for each: row matrix with one row, column matrix with one column, square matrix with as many rows as columns, diagonal matrix with zeros off the diagonal, scalar matrix with equal diagonal entries, identity matrix with ones on the diagonal, and zero matrix with every entry zero.
visual.caption: Every identity matrix is scalar, and every scalar matrix is diagonal.

visuals.alt: Decision chart for naming a matrix: if it is not square it is a row, column or rectangular matrix; if square, check whether all off-diagonal entries are zero; if not, it is just square; if yes, check whether the diagonal entries are equal: if not, it is diagonal; if yes, it is a scalar matrix, and the identity when the common value is 1.
visuals.caption: Square → diagonal → scalar → identity: each is a special case of the one before.

sections.heading: 3. Equality, addition and scalar multiplication
sections.body_md:
**Equality:** $A = B$ when they have the same order and $a_{ij} = b_{ij}$ for every $i$, $j$. One matrix equation gives one equation per position, e.g. $\begin{bmatrix} 2a & b + 1 \\ c - 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ 7 & d \end{bmatrix}$ gives $a = 3$, $b = -4$, $c = 9$, $d = 4$.

**Addition** (same order only): $A + B = [a_{ij} + b_{ij}]$. **Scalar multiple:** $kA = [k a_{ij}]$. **Difference:** $A - B = A + (-1)B$.

**Properties:** $A + B = B + A$; $(A + B) + C = A + (B + C)$; $A + O = A$; $A + (-A) = O$; $k(A + B) = kA + kB$; $(k + l)A = kA + lA$.

key_terms.definition_md: Same order and equal corresponding entries.
Multiplying every entry of a matrix by the same number.

visual.alt: Table of one canteen sales: Monday 60 samosas, 45 idlis and 30 juices; Tuesday 55, 50 and 35; the total row 115, 95 and 65 is obtained by adding corresponding entries.
visual.caption: Adding matrices adds corresponding entries.

rows: $k(A + B) = kA + kB$, $(k + l)A = kA + lA$

visuals.alt: Table of properties of addition and scalar multiplication for matrices of the same order: commutative, associative, the zero matrix as identity, negative matrix as inverse, and scalars distributing over sums.
visuals.caption: Addition behaves just like addition of numbers, entry by entry.

nodes.label: Equate each pair of corresponding entries

visuals.alt: Flow for equality of matrices: if the orders differ, the matrices are not equal; if the orders match, equate corresponding entries and solve the equations that result.
visuals.caption: Two matrices are equal only when they have the same order and the same entries.

sections.heading: 4. Multiplication of matrices
sections.body_md:
If $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times p$, then $AB$ is the $m \times p$ matrix with
$$c_{ik} = a_{i1}b_{1k} + a_{i2}b_{2k} + \dots + a_{in}b_{nk},$$
i.e. **row $i$ of $A$ times column $k$ of $B$**. If the inner numbers differ, $AB$ is not defined.

**Laws that hold:** $(AB)C = A(BC)$; $A(B + C) = AB + AC$; $(A + B)C = AC + BC$; $AI = IA = A$ for square $A$.

**Laws that fail:** $AB \ne BA$ in general (e.g. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$); $AB = O$ is possible with $A \ne O$, $B \ne O$; $(A + B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2$.

**Matrix polynomials:** for $f(x) = x^2 - 5x + 7$, $f(A) = A^2 - 5A + 7I$. For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ this is $O$.

A $2 \times 2$ matrix times a column $\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}$ moves the point $(x, y)$: the picture shows the unit square under $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Columns of the first matrix = rows of the second.

visual.alt: The unit square with corners O at the origin, P at 1 comma 0, Q at 1 comma 1 and R at 0 comma 1, shaded, and its image under the matrix with rows 2 1 and 0 1: a slanted parallelogram with corners O, P prime at 2 comma 0, Q prime at 3 comma 1 and R prime at 1 comma 1, which is the same point as Q.
visual.caption: Multiplying each corner by $M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ stretches and slants the square into a parallelogram.

visuals.alt: Flow for when a product is defined: A of order m by n and B of order n by p have matching inner numbers, so A B exists and has order m by p, the outer numbers.
visuals.caption: Inner numbers must match; outer numbers give the order.

visuals.alt: Table of the products A B and B A for A with rows 1 1 and 0 2 and B with rows 3 0 and 1 1: A B has rows 4 1 and 2 2, while B A has rows 3 3 and 1 3, so the two products are different.
visuals.caption: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: order matters.

visuals.alt: Table of properties of matrix multiplication: associative yes, distributive yes, identity yes for square matrices; commutative not in general; the zero-product rule fails; and the square of a sum expands with 2 A B only when A and B commute.
visuals.caption: Three rules carry over from numbers; three do not.

sections.heading: 5. Transpose
sections.body_md:
The **transpose** of $A = [a_{ij}]_{m \times n}$ is $A^T = [a_{ji}]_{n \times m}$: rows of $A$ become columns of $A^T$.

**Properties:** $(A^T)^T = A$; $(kA)^T = kA^T$; $(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T$; $(AB)^T = B^TA^T$ (**reversal law**).

Example: for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$, both $(AB)^T$ and $B^TA^T$ equal $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 7 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The matrix obtained by interchanging rows and columns.

visual.alt: A 2 by 3 matrix with rows 1 4 0 and minus 2 3 5, and its transpose, a 3 by 2 matrix whose columns are those rows: rows 1 minus 2, 4 3 and 0 5.
visual.caption: Rows of $A$ become columns of $A^T$.

visuals.alt: Table of the four properties of the transpose: transposing twice returns A; a scalar comes out; the transpose of a sum is the sum of transposes; the transpose of a product is the product of transposes in the reverse order.
visuals.caption: The order reverses only for products.

sections.heading: 6. Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
sections.body_md:
A square matrix is **symmetric** if $A^T = A$ ($a_{ji} = a_{ij}$) and **skew-symmetric** if $A^T = -A$ ($a_{ji} = -a_{ij}$). A skew-symmetric matrix has every diagonal entry $0$. Only $O$ is both.

**Theorem.** For any square $A$, $A + A^T$ is symmetric and $A - A^T$ is skew-symmetric, so
$$A = \underbrace{\tfrac12(A + A^T)}_{P\ \text{symmetric}} + \underbrace{\tfrac12(A - A^T)}_{Q\ \text{skew-symmetric}}.$$

Example: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.

visual.alt: Flow for splitting a square matrix: find A transpose; half of A plus A transpose is the symmetric part P; half of A minus A transpose is the skew-symmetric part Q; and P plus Q gives back A.
visual.caption: Every square matrix splits into a symmetric part and a skew-symmetric part.

visuals.alt: Table comparing symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices: symmetric means the transpose equals the matrix, mirror entries equal, example with rows 2 minus 1 4, minus 1 0 3, 4 3 5; skew-symmetric means the transpose equals the negative, mirror entries opposite and diagonal zero, example with rows 0 2 minus 6, minus 2 0 1, 6 minus 1 0.
visuals.caption: Mirror the matrix in its main diagonal: equal partners or opposite partners.

sections.heading: 7. Invertible matrices
sections.body_md:
A square matrix $A$ of order $n$ is **invertible** if there is a square matrix $B$ of order $n$ with $AB = BA = I$; $B$ is the inverse $A^{-1}$. Non-square matrices are never invertible, and some square matrices (such as $O$, or $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$) are not.

**Uniqueness.** If $B$ and $C$ are inverses of $A$: $B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C$.

**Finding or checking an inverse (this chapter):**
- *Verify* a given $B$: show $AB = I$ and $BA = I$.
- *Solve* $AB = I$ for unknown entries $p, q, r, s$: two pairs of linear equations, e.g. $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
- *From a relation:* if $A^2 - 5A + 7I = O$ then $A(5I - A) = 7I$, so $A^{-1} = \frac17(5I - A)$.

(The adjoint method comes in the chapter on determinants; elementary row operations are not in the 2026–27 syllabus.)

key_terms.definition_md: A square matrix with an inverse.

nodes.label: Suppose $B$ and $C$ are both inverses of $A$
So $B = C$: the inverse is unique

visual.alt: Proof chain for uniqueness of the inverse: start with B equals B times I, replace I by A C, regroup as B A times C by associativity, which is I times C, which is C; so B equals C.
visual.caption: Four short steps prove the inverse is unique.

visuals.alt: Table solving A B equals I for A with rows 2 5 and 1 3: the first column gives 2 p plus 5 r equals 1 and p plus 3 r equals 0, so r is minus 1 and p is 3; the second column gives 2 q plus 5 s equals 0 and q plus 3 s equals 1, so s is 2 and q is minus 5.
visuals.caption: So the inverse is $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

visuals.alt: Table of two square matrices: for the matrix with rows 4 3 and 1 1, the candidate with rows 1 minus 3 and minus 1 4 gives the identity both ways, so it is the inverse; the matrix with rows 1 2 and 2 4 sends the non-zero column 2, minus 1 to zero, so it has no inverse.
visuals.caption: A matrix that sends a non-zero column to $O$ cannot be undone, so it has no inverse.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Construct a matrix / equality (1–2 marks):* entries row by row; one equation per position.
- *Products and polynomials (2–5 marks):* order check, each row-by-column sum, final matrix; constant term as a multiple of $I$.
- *Symmetric + skew-symmetric (3–5 marks):* $A^T$, $P$, $Q$, checks that $P^T = P$, $Q^T = -Q$ and $P + Q = A$.
- *Inverse (2–5 marks):* both products $AB$ and $BA$; in relation questions show the rearrangement $A(\dots) = I$.
- *Proofs (2–3 marks):* uniqueness of the inverse; $A + A^T$ symmetric, $A - A^T$ skew-symmetric.

**Common mistakes**
1. Writing the order as columns × rows, or reading $a_{ij}$ as column $i$, row $j$.
2. Adding matrices of different orders.
3. Squaring each entry instead of computing $AA$.
4. Assuming $AB = BA$, or expanding $(A + B)^2$ with $2AB$.
5. Concluding $A = O$ or $B = O$ from $AB = O$.
6. $(AB)^T = A^TB^T$ (the order must reverse).
7. Forgetting the $\frac12$ when splitting into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts.
8. Writing a number instead of a multiple of $I$ in a matrix polynomial.

questions.stem_md: A matrix with 3 rows and 4 columns has order
questions.solution_md: Order is written (number of rows) $\times$ (number of columns), so it is $3 \times 4$. It has $12$ elements, but $12$ is not its order.

questions.stem_md: A matrix has exactly 12 elements. How many different orders can it have?
questions.solution_md: An $m \times n$ matrix has $mn$ elements, so $mn = 12$: $1 \times 12$, $12 \times 1$, $2 \times 6$, $6 \times 2$, $3 \times 4$, $4 \times 3$. That is $6$ orders (one for each divisor of $12$).

questions.stem_md: The matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ is best described as
questions.solution_md: It is square, its off-diagonal elements are $0$ and its diagonal elements are equal ($4$), so it is a scalar matrix, $4I$. It is not the identity matrix because the diagonal elements are not $1$.

questions.stem_md: A $2 \times 3$ matrix $A = [a_{ij}]$ has $a_{ij} = 2i - j$. The element $a_{23}$ is
questions.solution_md: $a_{23}$ is in row $i = 2$, column $j = 3$: $a_{23} = 2(2) - 3 = 1$. Option (a) uses $i = 3$, $j = 2$, which does not even exist in a $2 \times 3$ matrix.

questions.stem_md: If $\begin{bmatrix} x + y & 3 \\ 1 & x - y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then
questions.solution_md: Equal matrices have equal corresponding elements: $x + y = 7$ and $x - y = 1$. Adding, $2x = 8$, so $x = 4$ and $y = 3$.

questions.stem_md: If $A$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix and $B$ is a $3 \times 4$ matrix, then $AB$ is
questions.solution_md: $AB$ is defined because $A$ has $3$ columns and $B$ has $3$ rows. The product takes the rows of $A$ and the columns of $B$: order $2 \times 4$.

questions.stem_md: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$ equals
questions.solution_md: A $1 \times 2$ matrix times a $2 \times 1$ matrix is $1 \times 1$: $1(3) + 2(-1) = 1$. Option (a) is the product in the other order, column times row.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, then $A^2$ is
questions.solution_md: Row 1 times column 2: $2(1) + 1(3) = 5$; the other entries are $4$, $0$, $9$. Option (a) squares each entry, which is not matrix multiplication; option (b) is $2A$.

questions.stem_md: For any two square matrices A and B of the same order, which statement is always true?
questions.solution_md: Matrix addition is commutative because it adds corresponding elements. Multiplication is not commutative, so $(A + B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2$, which need not equal $A^2 + 2AB + B^2$; and two non-zero matrices can have a zero product.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A^2 = kA$, then $k$ equals
questions.solution_md: $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 8 \\ 8 & 8 \end{bmatrix} = 4A$, so $k = 4$. Option (d) is an entry of $A^2$, not the multiplier.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, then $A^4$ equals
questions.solution_md: $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = -I$, so $A^4 = (A^2)^2 = (-I)^2 = I$.

questions.stem_md: For matrices $A$ and $B$ for which $AB$ is defined, $(AB)^T$ equals
questions.solution_md: The reversal law: the transpose of a product is the product of the transposes in the reverse order, $(AB)^T = B^TA^T$. In general $A^TB^T$ is different and may not even be defined.

questions.stem_md: The diagonal elements of a skew-symmetric matrix are

options.text_md: equal to each other but non-zero

questions.solution_md: Skew-symmetric means $a_{ji} = -a_{ij}$ for all $i$, $j$. With $j = i$: $a_{ii} = -a_{ii}$, so $2a_{ii} = 0$ and $a_{ii} = 0$.

questions.stem_md: The matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 & -2 \\ x & 0 & 5 \\ 2 & -5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ is skew-symmetric when $x$ equals
questions.solution_md: Skew-symmetric needs $a_{21} = -a_{12}$, so $x = -3$. The other pairs already satisfy the condition: $a_{31} = 2 = -(-2)$ and $a_{32} = -5 = -5$, and the diagonal is zero.

questions.stem_md: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, the symmetric matrix $\dfrac12(A + A^T)$ is
questions.solution_md: $A + A^T = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 6 \\ 6 & -4 \end{bmatrix}$; halving gives option (c). Option (d) is the skew-symmetric part, (a) forgets the half and (b) is just $A^T$.

questions.stem_md: A square matrix $A$ has inverse $B$. Which statement must hold?
questions.solution_md: By definition, $B$ is the inverse of the square matrix $A$ when $AB = BA = I$, with $I$ the identity matrix of the same order.

questions.stem_md: The inverse of $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ is

questions.stem_md: A square matrix $A$ satisfies $A^2 - 4A + I = O$. Then $A^{-1}$ equals
questions.solution_md: Rewrite as $I = 4A - A^2 = A(4I - A)$. Similarly $(4I - A)A = I$. So $A^{-1} = 4I - A$. (For instance $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ satisfies the relation and its inverse is $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.)

questions.stem_md: $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix. Both $AB$ and $BA$ are defined. The order of $B$ is
questions.solution_md: $AB$ defined: $B$ has $2$ rows (the columns of $A$). $BA$ defined: $B$ has $3$ columns (the rows of $A$). So $B$ is $2 \times 3$.

By associativity, $B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C$.
So $B = C$: the inverse, when it exists, is unique.

(b) Hence find $A^{-1}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 + 1 & -2 - 2 \\ -2 - 2 & 1 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$. $4A = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -4 \\ -4 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$, $3I = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. So $A^2 - 4A + 3I = \begin{bmatrix} 5 - 8 + 3 & -4 + 4 + 0 \\ -4 + 4 + 0 & 5 - 8 + 3 \end{bmatrix} = O$.

(b) $3I = 4A - A^2 = A(4I - A)$, so $A \cdot \dfrac13(4I - A) = I$; similarly $\dfrac13(4I - A) \cdot A = I$. Hence
$A^{-1} = \dfrac13(4I - A) = \dfrac13\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \end{bmatrix}$.

(c) $AA^{-1} = \dfrac13\begin{bmatrix} 4 - 1 & 2 - 2 \\ -2 + 2 & -1 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac13\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = I$.

questions.stem_md:
For a real number $a$, let $E(a) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

(a) Prove that $E(a)E(b) = E(a + b)$ for all real $a$, $b$.

(b) Deduce that $E(a)E(b) = E(b)E(a)$, although matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

(c) Show that $E(a)$ is invertible and find its inverse.

(d) Find $E(3)^5$ and the value of $n$ for which $E(2)^n = E(18)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $E(a)E(b) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cdot 1 + a \cdot 0 & 1 \cdot b + a \cdot 1 \\ 0 + 0 & 0 \cdot b + 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a + b \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = E(a + b)$.

(b) $E(a)E(b) = E(a + b) = E(b + a) = E(b)E(a)$, using (a) twice and $a + b = b + a$. These particular matrices commute even though matrices in general do not.

(c) $E(a)E(-a) = E(0) = I$ and $E(-a)E(a) = E(0) = I$, so $E(a)$ is invertible with $E(a)^{-1} = E(-a) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -a \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

(d) By (a) repeatedly, $E(3)^5 = E(15) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 15 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Similarly $E(2)^n = E(2n) = E(18)$ gives $2n = 18$, $n = 9$.

questions.solution_md: Multiply the general matrices once; every later part follows from the rule E(a)E(b) = E(a + b).

Canteen A sold $60$ samosas, $45$ idlis and $30$ juices; canteen B sold $50$ samosas, $70$ idlis and $40$ juices. The sales matrix $S$ has the canteens as rows and the items as columns. Both canteens charge ₹$15$ for a samosa, ₹$20$ for an idli and ₹$25$ for a juice, written as the column matrix $P$. On Tuesday the sales matrix was $T = \begin{bmatrix} 55 & 50 & 35 \\ 45 & 60 & 50 \end{bmatrix}$.

children.stem_md: The order of the sales matrix S is
How many idlis did the two canteens sell together on Monday?

answer.model_answer_md: $S + T = \begin{bmatrix} 115 & 95 & 65 \\ 95 & 130 & 90 \end{bmatrix}$. Row sums: A $115 + 95 + 65 = 275$, B $95 + 130 + 90 = 315$. Canteen B sold more items.

questions.passage_md: A dairy cooperative near Anand delivers full-cream and toned milk every morning to two cities. Surat receives $200$ litres of full-cream and $300$ litres of toned milk; Vadodara receives $150$ litres of full-cream and $250$ litres of toned milk. This is recorded as $Q = \begin{bmatrix} 200 & 300 \\ 150 & 250 \end{bmatrix}$ (rows: Surat, Vadodara; columns: full-cream, toned). The prices per litre are ₹$64$ (full-cream) and ₹$52$ (toned), written as $P = \begin{bmatrix} 64 \\ 52 \end{bmatrix}$.

children.stem_md: Which product gives the daily bill of each city as a column matrix?
children.solution_md: $QP$ is $2 \times 1$: each row of $Q$ (a city's litres) times the price column. $PQ$ is not defined; $P^TP$ is $1 \times 1$; $P^TQ^T$ is a $1 \times 2$ row, not a column.

children.stem_md: **(i)** Both prices rise by ₹$4$ per litre. Find the new daily bill matrix and each city's increase.

answer.model_answer_md: New price matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 68 \\ 56 \end{bmatrix}$. New bills: $\begin{bmatrix} 200(68) + 300(56) \\ 150(68) + 250(56) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 13600 + 16800 \\ 10200 + 14000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 30400 \\ 24200 \end{bmatrix}$. Old bills $\begin{bmatrix} 28400 \\ 22600 \end{bmatrix}$, so Surat pays ₹$2000$ more and Vadodara ₹$1600$ more ($4$ times the litres each city receives).

children.solution_md: Add 4 to each price, multiply again, subtract the old bills.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** Deliveries and prices stay the same for a week of $7$ days. Write the weekly bill matrix as a scalar multiple and evaluate it.

answer.model_answer_md: Weekly bill $= 7(QP) = 7\begin{bmatrix} 28400 \\ 22600 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 198800 \\ 158200 \end{bmatrix}$: Surat ₹$1{,}98{,}800$, Vadodara ₹$1{,}58{,}200$.

alternatives.solution_md: Multiply the daily bill matrix by 7.

questions.passage_md:
A football coach in Kolkata records passes between three midfielders in a practice match as a matrix $M = [m_{ij}]$, where $m_{ij}$ is the number of passes from player $i$ to player $j$:
$$M = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 7 & 4 \\ 5 & 0 & 6 \\ 2 & 9 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
So player 1 passed $7$ times to player 2, and received $5$ passes from player 2.

children.stem_md: The element in row 1, column 2 of $M^T$ is
children.solution_md: Transposing swaps the indices: $(M^T)_{12} = m_{21} = 5$, the passes player 1 **received** from player 2.

children.stem_md: Find the element in row 2, column 3 of $S = \frac12(M + M^T)$.
children.solution_md: $\dfrac12(m_{23} + m_{32}) = \dfrac12(6 + 9) = 7.5$: the average number of passes between players 2 and 3 in each direction.

children.stem_md: **(i)** Write $S = \frac12(M + M^T)$ and $K = \frac12(M - M^T)$, and check that $S + K = M$.

answer.model_answer_md: $M^T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 & 2 \\ 7 & 0 & 9 \\ 4 & 6 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$. $S = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 6 & 3 \\ 6 & 0 & 7.5 \\ 3 & 7.5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ (symmetric), $K = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1.5 \\ -1 & 1.5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ (skew-symmetric). Adding gives $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 7 & 4 \\ 5 & 0 & 6 \\ 2 & 9 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = M$.

children.solution_md: Transpose first, then halve the sum and the difference.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** Find $M - M^T$, show that it is skew-symmetric, and use it to say which player made more passes in each pair.

answer.model_answer_md: $M - M^T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & -3 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$. Its transpose is its negative, so it is skew-symmetric. A positive entry in row $i$, column $j$ means player $i$ passed more to $j$ than $j$ passed back: player 1 made $2$ more passes than player 2 and $2$ more than player 3 in those pairs; player 3 made $3$ more than player 2.

alternatives.solution_md: Read the positive entries of the difference.

questions.passage_md: Students of a coding club in Bhopal send secret two-letter messages. Each letter is replaced by its position in the alphabet (A = 1, B = 2, …, Z = 26), and a pair of letters is written as a column matrix $X$. The sender transmits $Y = EX$, where the encoding matrix is $E = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. The receiver recovers $X = DY$ using a decoding matrix $D$ with $DE = ED = I$.

children.solution_md: $E\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 3 & -2 + 2 \\ 6 - 6 & -3 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = I$. Option (a) gives $-I$ and option (b) is the transpose of the correct matrix, which does not work.

children.stem_md: The word GO is $X = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix}$. Find the first entry of the transmitted matrix $Y = EX$.
children.solution_md: Row 1 of $E$ times $X$: $2(7) + 1(15) = 29$. (The second entry is $3(7) + 2(15) = 51$.)

children.stem_md: **(i)** The receiver gets $Y = \begin{bmatrix} 25 \\ 42 \end{bmatrix}$. Decode the message.

answer.model_answer_md: $X = DY = \begin{bmatrix} 2(25) - 1(42) \\ -3(25) + 2(42) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 50 - 42 \\ -75 + 84 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}$. Letters 8 and 9 are H and I: the message is HI.

children.solution_md: Multiply by the decoding matrix, then convert numbers to letters.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** Show that $ED = I$ and $DE = I$ for $D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, so $D = E^{-1}$.

answer.model_answer_md: $ED = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 3 & -2 + 2 \\ 6 - 6 & -3 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $DE = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 3 & 2 - 2 \\ -6 + 6 & -3 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Both products are $I$, so $D = E^{-1}$.

alternatives.solution_md: Both orders of multiplication are needed.
